clue.text: Going to the dogs?

parts.note: the idiom for decline is read literally: riders following a pack of foxhounds are heading after the dogs

explanation.surface: A lament that everything is in decline.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'going to the dogs' means deteriorating; here it is taken as a literal journey after the hounds in a fox hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunting on horseback means following a pack, travelling where the hunting dogs lead.

clue.text: Story with a poor beginning but a capital ending

definitions.text: Story with a poor beginning but a capital ending

parts.words: Story with a poor beginning but a capital ending
parts.note: capital means both excellent and money, so the tale starts in poverty and finishes in wealth

explanation.surface: A literary critique of a tale that starts badly but finishes splendidly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' and 'capital' read as judgments of quality, but they mean penniless and moneyed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a tale of someone rising from poverty to great wealth.

clue.text: Give a name to first-class city of Arabia

parts.note: to dub someone is to give them a name or title
A1 (written AI) means first-class

explanation.surface: An instruction to name a top-rank Arabian city.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubai is a major city of the United Arab Emirates, on the Arabian peninsula.

clue.text: Ran up share account

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word ran is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a ration is an allotted share

explanation.surface: Someone ran up their portion of a shared account, as in a bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran up' looks like running up a bill; 'up' is the reversal sign, giving NAR.
explanation.definitionFit: An account of events is a telling or narrative of them.

clue.text: Soldiers welcome sailors inside foreign restaurant

indicators.note: inside says the greeting and the navy go within the army letters

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's reserve soldiers
ave is a Latin greeting, hail or welcome
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: Troops greet visiting navy men in a restaurant abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army is Britain's volunteer reserve force; 'welcome' is the Latin greeting, and 'inside' puts it and the navy within the soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A taverna is a small Greek eating house, so a restaurant from abroad.

clue.text: The bare ingredients of a brew up

indicators.note: the letters of the bare are the components to be mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Listing the simplest constituents of a pot of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ingredients of' signals that THEBARE is rearranged. A brew-up is British slang for making tea.
explanation.definitionFit: An infusion of leaves such as mint or camomile is a kind of tea, a brew.

clue.text: A lump in one's throat

parts.note: the idiom for being choked with emotion is read as an actual fleshy lobe at the back of the mouth

explanation.surface: Feeling choked up with emotion.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom suggests tearfulness; taken literally it is the soft dangling part at the back of the throat.
explanation.definitionFit: This small fleshy projection hangs from the soft palate at the back of the mouth.

clue.text: Paper said to come out and leave no trace

indicators.note: the letters of paper said are to emerge in a different arrangement

explanation.surface: A newspaper announced it would publish and then vanish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come out' looks like publication; it signals rearranging PAPERSAID.
explanation.definitionFit: To vanish is to go away without a sign of having been there.

clue.text: Yachtsman changing course heard to be the one jeering

indicators.note: heard says the word for the sailor is spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: to gybe is to swing a sail across when changing course downwind, so a sailor doing so is a gyber

explanation.surface: A yachtsman tacking about is mocked by an onlooker.
explanation.walkthrough: A gybe is a sailing manoeuvre; one who gybes sounds the same as one who gibes, or mocks.
explanation.definitionFit: To gibe is to jeer or taunt, so one who does it is a mocker.

clue.text: Ivor's out to become a skilled performer

indicators.note: the letters of Ivor's out turn into a new word, signalling rearrangement

explanation.surface: Ivor has gone out in pursuit of becoming an expert player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like the indicator but is part of the fodder IVORSOUT; 'to become' does the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: A virtuoso is a performer, usually a musician, of exceptional technical skill.

clue.text: One looking for scraps may show it

definitions.text: One looking for scraps may show it

parts.words: One looking for scraps may show it
parts.note: scraps reads like leftover food, but means fights, so a scrapper shows aggression

explanation.surface: A hungry scavenger, such as a stray dog hunting leftovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scraps' suggests morsels of food; here it means fights.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggressiveness or eagerness to fight is what a quarrelsome person displays.

clue.text: Might one disappear into it at the top of Everest?

definitions.text: Might one disappear into it at the top of Everest?

parts.words: Might one disappear into it at the top of Everest?
parts.note: the idiom for vanishing completely meets the rarefied atmosphere at high altitude

explanation.surface: A climber vanishing on the summit of the world's highest mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: To vanish 'into thin air' is an idiom; at high altitude the atmosphere really is rarefied.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for vanishing without a trace, and literally the low-oxygen atmosphere at great height.

clue.text: Tramp a priest converted

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A vagrant turned a clergyman to the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' looks like a noun, a vagrant, but is the verb, to trudge; 'converted' rearranges APRIEST.
explanation.definitionFit: To trudge wearily or wander about on foot is the same as to tramp.

clue.text: Teacher's pet is short of time

indicators.note: is short of means lacking, so a letter is dropped from the pet

parts.note: a rabbit is a common household pet

explanation.surface: The teacher's favourite pupil has run out of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teacher's pet' reads as a favoured pupil; 'Teacher' is the definition and 'pet' gives RABBIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish scholar and religious teacher.

clue.text: Wish for a pleasant journey from France

definitions.text: Wish for a pleasant journey from France

parts.words: Wish for a pleasant journey from France
parts.note: from France means the farewell is in French, not that the trip starts there

explanation.surface: Hoping for a pleasant trip departing from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From France' seems to give the starting point; it means the phrase is French.
explanation.definitionFit: The French farewell to travellers literally means good journey.

clue.text: One ringing to warn you of danger?

definitions.text: One ringing to warn you of danger?

parts.words: One ringing to warn you of danger?
parts.note: reads as a person phoning with a warning, but it is a device that rings

explanation.surface: A friend phoning to tip you off about a threat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One ringing' suggests a caller on the phone; it is a bell that rings itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A warning signal device that sounds when there is fire or intrusion.

clue.text: Form of variety before the '50s, much as I recollected

indicators.note: before places the rearranged letters ahead of the fifties letters
recollected, read as re-collected, means gathered up again in a new order

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, so fifties in the plural are two of them

explanation.surface: A popular entertainment before the 1950s, as remembered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recollected' looks like memory but rearranges MUCHASI; the '50s gives LL, two Roman fifties. Music hall was British variety theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Variety is popular stage entertainment of mixed acts, and British music hall was one form of it.

clue.text: Fool holds sister with strange puzzle

indicators.note: holds means the fool letters enclose the sister

parts.note: cod is an old verb meaning to fool or hoax
a nun is a religious sister
rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: An idiot keeps his sister with him in a baffling situation.
explanation.walkthrough: COD, to hoax, holds NUN; RUM is British slang for odd.
explanation.definitionFit: A conundrum is a riddle or problem that is hard to solve.

clue.text: A target set out for meeting at sea

indicators.note: set out means laid out afresh, so the letters are arranged differently

explanation.surface: A goal is established for an encounter on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' looks like establishing a target; it rearranges ATARGET.
explanation.definitionFit: A regatta is a series of boat races, an event or meeting on the water.

clue.text: Turn, or intend to turn, Communist

parts.note: to mean something is to intend it

indicators.note: to turn means the word for communist is reversed, read upwards here

parts.note: red is a common term for a communist

explanation.surface: Someone changes, or plans to change, political allegiance to communism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' appears twice: the first is the definition, the second reverses RED.
explanation.definitionFit: A river's winding bend, or to wander a winding course, is a turn.

clue.text: Head of school, goody-goody young man

indicators.note: head of means the opening letter of the word school

parts.note: a prig is a smugly self-righteous goody-goody

explanation.surface: A school's head pupil is a prim, virtuous youth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of school' looks like a headteacher; it gives only S.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprig, in a dated usage, is a youngster, a young man.

clue.text: Leaving unannounced for an away match

definitions.text: Leaving unannounced for an away match

parts.words: Leaving unannounced for an away match
parts.note: match suggests a sports fixture, but here is a marriage held away from home after secretly leaving

explanation.surface: A player slipping off quietly to a game at another ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Away match' suggests sport; the match is a wedding made by running off in secret.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovers who run off secretly to marry are said to do this.

clue.text: Warm place in the singing lesson

indicators.note: in says the answer lies within the words singing lesson

explanation.surface: A cosy spot where a singing class is held.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingle is a fireside or chimney corner, a warm spot by the hearth.

clue.text: He charges a couple of hundred to the employer

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so two of them
one who uses something employs it, so a user is an employer

explanation.surface: A man bills his boss two hundred pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' looks like billing, but it is making accusations; 'employer' is one who employs, or uses, something.
explanation.definitionFit: One who charges another with a crime or fault is an accuser.

clue.text: Open return to southern country

indicators.note: return means the word for open is turned back, read upwards in this down clue

parts.note: airy means open, spacious, well ventilated

explanation.surface: A frank homecoming to a country in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' reverses the word for open, giving YRIA, which follows the southern letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Syria is a country in the Middle East.

clue.text: After Greta perhaps, Ted identified as a victim

indicators.note: after places the name Ted at the end
perhaps suggests Greta is one possible arrangement of these letters

explanation.surface: Following Greta, Ted is singled out as the next target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' says the name Greta is just one arrangement of the letters, which become TARGE; 'After' puts the second name last.
explanation.definitionFit: Singled out for attack is what being aimed at, made a target, means.

clue.text: Protection with strings attached

parts.note: strings attached suggests conditions, but this protective garment is literally tied on with strings

explanation.surface: A security deal that comes with conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strings attached' sounds like hidden conditions; here it is the ties on a kitchen garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A garment tied at the waist and neck that protects clothes while cooking.

clue.text: Grant free film in circulation

parts.note: Ulysses S. Grant was a Union general in the American Civil War
to release is to set free

explanation.surface: Granting a free film showing to the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' looks like a verb, to give; it is General Grant of the American Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: A movie on wide distribution to cinemas everywhere is said to be on this.
